rashi:a1.1: From Kefar Otnai to Kefar Ḥananya is thirty-two mil, and Tzippori, in the middle, combines them.
rashi:a2.1: Shmuel interpreted it in accordance with Rav: when the baraita teaches “one in the middle,” it does not refer to the first clause, which deals with five [on each side], but to a case where he has nine from here and nine from there, etc.
rashi:a3.1: And according to Shmuel: who does not require that the animals in the middle be fit to complete the count, even a shepherd who has a dwelling in the middle, and has no animal there at all, combines them.
rashi:a3.2: And even the implements of the shepherd: if they are lying in that village, they combine them, since the shepherd will eventually go there and take them, and we apply to him “who counts them.”
rashi:a4.1: That he calls it and it comes: and the shepherd need not go there, so we do not apply to him “who counts them.”
rashi:a6.1: That are not close: neither the animals nor the shepherd can go from one to the other.
rashi:a6.2: Avtilaot: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss) two provinces within one kingdom.
rashi:a6.3: Namer and Namori: two avtilaot. [Flocks in them] do not combine, even though they are within one mil of each other.
rashi:a7.1: Is like a place that has a bridge: for there is no river there, and yet it teaches that outside the Land and the Land of Israel, [even] if they all stand within one mil, but this one is in the Land and that one outside it, they do not combine.
rashi:a8.1: “And the Jordan shall border it”: in the book of Joshua (chapter 18), at the border of one of the tribes.
rashi:a9.1: But if that is so: everywhere in the inheritance of the tribes it is written “and the border was drawn,” so here too each tribe would be a border by itself, and if he has [animals] in the inheritance of this tribe and in the inheritance of that tribe, they would not combine, even within sixteen mil. If so, why did [the baraita] mention outside the Land and the Land?
rashi:a10.1: “This shall be your land,” etc.: after [the verse] listed all of them, it made it one land.
rashi:a10.2: “Land”: the verse writes “this shall be your land”; the borders of the land count as one, but not the borders of the Jordan.
rashi:a12.1: According to Rabbi Ami: who said it is because they are distant [from each other], let it teach: all rivers divide.
rashi:a13.1: Let us say it is like a dispute of tanna’im: whether the Jordan counts as the land of Canaan and does not divide, or not.
rashi:a15.1: From Beit Jericho and below: but all that stretches above Jericho is not the Jordan, since its distinction is nullified as it mixes into great seas.
rashi:a15.2: For one who vows: that one who vows [to abstain] from the Jordan would be permitted to drink from Jericho upward.
rashi:a17.1: From Dan: the name of a place.
rashi:a17.2: You [learned it]: from an inference from the name “Jordan” you learn it.
rashi:a17.3: From the Cave of Pamyas: evidently it comes from Dan.
rashi:a18.1: Zakhruteih of the Jordan: the source of the Jordan.
rashi:a19.1: The source of blood: the root of the blood is the liver.
rashi:a19.3: With a quarter-log: under the law of the blood of a corpse.
rashi:a21.1: I will not drink from the waters of the Euphrates: he means the waters called “Euphrates,” and one follows the language of people, for a person who vows has in mind only the name he is used to calling that place.
rashi:a22.1: All the rivers: in the world are below, except for three rivers, the Tigris, the Pishon and the Gihon; for all the rivers in the world come from there.
tosafot:a8.1: The verse states: “And the Jordan shall border it on the east side”: this is written of the border of Benjamin in the book of Joshua, and not as it is written in [some] books.
tosafot:a10.1: There it is different, as the verse states: “This shall be your land according to its borders round about”: this verse is written in the portion of Ele Mas’ei [Numbers 34], while the verses above, “and the border was drawn” and “and the border went up,” are written in the book of Joshua, [describing] the division of each tribe. The verse of Mas’ei teaches us that the whole border of the Land of Israel is one. It is not as the Kuntres [Rashi] explained, “after it listed them all, it made it one land,” which implies that both are written in one place; that is not so, as this one is written in the Torah and that one in the Prophets.
tosafot:a14.1: It is written “beyond the Jordan at Jericho eastward, toward the sunrise”; just as Jericho is the land [of Canaan], etc.: And if you say: if he expounds from the juxtaposition of “Jordan” and “Jericho,” that is written in many places [so why this verse]? One may say that he cites this verse specifically, since it is written in Mas’ei after [the Torah] listed the boundaries of the Land of Israel, and it is written there, “And Moses commanded,” etc., up to “the two tribes and the half tribe have received their inheritance beyond the Jordan at Jericho eastward, toward the sunrise.” This implies that the Jordan was part of the essential Land of Israel and not included in the border of the two tribes, just as Jericho is not included in their border.
tosafot:a15.1: In brief: The river is called Jordan only from Beit Jericho and below. The Kuntres [Rashi] explained that above Jericho it is not the Jordan, since its distinction is nullified as it mixes into great seas. This is difficult: if it loses its distinction above because it mixes, it should lose it below too, since it has already mixed in the seas above. One may answer that although it mixed above, below it can emerge from the waters and flow without mixture, as the baraita here says it passes through the Sea of Sivkhi, the Sea of Tiberias and the Sea of Sodom and falls into the Great Sea, implying that it is recognizable as it leaves each of them; and Bereshit Rabba likewise says the Jordan passes through the Salt Sea without mixing. Still it is difficult for Rashi’s explanation: one could just as well say it loses its distinction below Jericho, where it widens and goes into the Salt Sea. [Tosafot then traces the tribal borders from Joshua 15 and 18: Judah held the south, the children of Joseph the north and Benjamin the middle; the Salt Sea lay on Judah’s east; the Jordan was Benjamin’s eastern border (“And the Jordan shall border it on the east side”); Benjamin’s northern line runs from the Jordan up the shoulder of Jericho on the north, so Jericho lay inside Benjamin; and its southern border ends at the tongue of the Salt Sea “at the end of the Jordan.”] All the verses show that the Jordan flowed from north to south and fell into the Salt Sea at the southern end of Benjamin’s border, with Jericho on Benjamin’s north side. So why should the Jordan lack distinction from Jericho upward, when there are no seas there until the end of Benjamin’s border? Rather, it seems the Gemara expounds a verse: it is called Jordan only from Beit Jericho and below because the verse “And the Jordan shall border it” speaks of the stretch from Beit Jericho and below. gershom:a1.1: Rav said: five from here, five from there and five in the middle. For these five are fit to combine both here and there: when the shepherd goes to those in the middle, his eye commands sixteen mil this way and sixteen mil that way, and they combine, for we apply to him “who counts them,” since he can see here and there.
gershom:a2.1: Tzippori stands between Kefar Ḥananya and Kefar Otnai, and among all three it is only thirty-two mil.
gershom:a3.1: A refutation of Rav, who said we require five in the middle, so that they are fit to combine here and there.
gershom:a4.1: Shmuel interpreted it, etc. And one in the middle: for that one is fit to combine here and there.
gershom:a5.1: Even the shepherd, and even his implements: that is, do not say that only when an animal is in the middle does it combine; even if the shepherd or his implements stand in the middle, they combine, since he can see here and there. And his implements: since when he comes to bring his implements that stand in the middle, his eye commands here and there.
gershom:a6.1: The shepherd’s dog: standing in the middle; does it combine or not?
gershom:a7.1: Since he calls the dog and it comes to him, and the shepherd need not go to it to bring it, he does not go there to the middle and his eye does not command here and there, so it does not combine them. Or perhaps, etc.
gershom:a8.1: Apparently: what it says, that the Jordan divides, is because they are not close, where there is no bridge, since these cannot come near those.
gershom:a9.1: Avtilaot [spelled avlatot in his text]: large cities.
gershom:a10.1: Is like a place that has a bridge: since there is no water between them and these can go to those, and yet they do not combine.
gershom:a11.1: It made it a border by itself: and it divides. So too, if he has animals in the borders of two tribes, they would not combine.
gershom:a12.1: All of the Land of Israel is one border: and they combine.
gershom:a13.1: If so, the Jordan too: is part of the Land of Israel, and it should not divide.
gershom:a14.1: Granted according to Rabbi Ḥiyya, who said it is because the Jordan is called a border; that is why it teaches “the Jordan divides.” But according to Rabbi Ami, who said it is because they are not close, let it teach simply: any river divides.
gershom:a15.1: If we say for one who vows: not to drink from the Jordan.
gershom:a16.1: And anywhere that they call it Jordan: whether below or above, it should be forbidden.
gershom:a17.1: Rather, for animal tithe: to divide, for it divides only from Beit Jericho and below.
gershom:a18.1: Zakhruteih: the source of the Jordan, from where it grows, that is, from the Cave of Pamyas.
gershom:a19.1: Imparts impurity with a quarter-log: like the law of the blood of a corpse.
gershom:a20.1: Dakhruta of the waters: the source of all the waters of the world is the Euphrates; they issue from it.
gershom:a21.1: And three rivers: the Gihon, the Pishon and the Tigris.
gershom:a22.1: Below the Euphrates: that is, all the waters issue from it.
rashi:b1.1: Springs that are high: springs of water that well up in high mountains; those are higher than the Euphrates, so how do they come from the Euphrates?
rashi:b1.2: Ladders of the Euphrates: they stream beneath the ground and rise up into the mountains like a ladder.
rashi:b2.1: “And the fourth river”: it counts [the Euphrates] as one of them, and you say they come from it?
rashi:b3.1: It is the Euphrates from the beginning: it is the Euphrates mentioned above, “And a river went out of Eden,” etc., from which the three separate.
rashi:b4.1: Yuval is its name: of the Euphrates. “And that spreads out its roots by the yuval”: the verse speaks of the Tree of Life, and the Tree of Life is in the Garden of Eden, and the Euphrates is what waters the Garden of Eden.
rashi:b4.2: Fruitful and multiply: it grows and multiplies without any rain.
rashi:b5.1: The great witness is the Euphrates: the Euphrates flows down from the Land of Israel to Babylonia, and when rains fall in the Land of Israel, the Euphrates in Babylonia is a great witness that rain fell in the West, since it grows on account of the rains.
rashi:b6.1: A ritual bath in the days of Nisan: a ritual bath of living, spring water in the house. He would not let them immerse in the rivers, since in the rainy season much rain fell, and he was concerned lest the water dripping from the clouds into the river exceed the flowing [spring water], and [the river] would not be fit for them, since they had the status of possible zavot, and of a zav it is written “living water” [Leviticus 15:13]. Another version: “exceed the flowing” refers to [rainwater] that fell from the clouds to the ground and from the ground crept and streamed into the river; for if it were not dripping [rainwater], it would not be disqualified on account of flowing, as we say in the first chapter of Temura (12a): drawn water is purified by being channeled, that is, one channels drawn water into the ritual bath through pipes.
rashi:b7.1: And mats in the days of Tishrei: when they immersed in the river in the days of Tishrei, he made them mats of reeds (Rashi adds an Old French gloss) and threw them into the water, and they stood on them and immersed. For in the days of Tishrei there is soft mud in the rivers near the bank, and he was concerned lest mud come up on their feet and be an interposition.
rashi:b8.1: This is the reading: “And it disagrees with his own”: that is, Shmuel’s [statement] disagrees with Shmuel’s.
rashi:b8.2: Water does not purify when flowing: for at all times the dripping [rain] water is more than it.
rashi:b8.3: Except the Euphrates in the days of Tishrei: for the waters of the Euphrates are fruitful and multiply, and the flowing waters that well up from springs are abundant; moreover, Tishrei is the end of the summer, and no rain has fallen for a long time. Evidently rivers increase from rainwater, whereas above he said the river is blessed from its bed. Another version: Shmuel’s father made ritual baths for his daughters in the days of Nisan, since that is the end of the winter, when much rain has fallen, but in the middle of the winter he did not; and this disagrees with Shmuel, who says that at all times we require ritual baths, except the Euphrates in the days of Tishrei.
tosafot:b3.1: It is the Euphrates from the beginning: that is, it is not because it is small that [the verse] calls it the fourth, for it is the original Euphrates, called Euphrates before it begins to divide into four heads. When it begins to divide, the rivers go out, one to this side and one to that side, and the Euphrates continues straight on its course. And in the portion of Shekalim, Rabbi Elazar HaKalir composed in the silluk that the Euphrates’ strength equals two rivers. So too it is implied in Bereshit Rabba that it is great: they say to the Euphrates, “Why is your voice not heard?” and it answers, “My fruits testify for me”; they say to the Tigris, “Why is your voice heard?” and it answers, “If only I could make my voice heard and be seen.” This implies that the Tigris is smaller than the Euphrates. It is somewhat difficult, for it says in the chapter Kol HaNishba’in (Shevuot 47b) on “the great river, the river Euphrates”: a king’s servant is like a king; this implies that it is called great only on account of the Land of Israel.
tosafot:b5.1: This supports Shmuel, as Shmuel says the river is blessed from its bed: Although Shmuel speaks of all rivers, while Rabbi Meir implies that it is the Euphrates specifically that is named Perat because its waters are fruitful and multiply, that is only because the Euphrates is blessed more, being more important than the others. Alternatively, because it is the head of them all, it is called Perat, since all are blessed from the bed of the Euphrates. And so Rabbeinu Tam explained in a responsum: since the Euphrates is above all the rivers and is high, and all the rivers drink from it, the verse attributed fruitfulness and multiplying to it, for when it increases, all the rivers increase.
tosafot:b5.2: Is blessed from its bed [mikefeih]: from its rock, as the Aramaic translation renders sela, rock, as kefa.
tosafot:b5.3: In brief: “Rain in the West, the great witness is the Euphrates”: here it is implied that the Euphrates flows from the Land of Israel to Babylonia, as explained above (Bekhorot 44b). It follows that the Garden of Eden is in the west of the world: Babylonia lies northeast of the Land of Israel, which is why the Babylonians call the Land of Israel “the West,” and Bava Batra 25b says Babylonia lies to the north (“Out of the north the evil shall break forth”). So the Euphrates flows from west to east, and so from its very source, since “it is the Euphrates from the beginning”; hence Eden is in the west. Bereshit Rabba implies the same: the east always receives — Adam (“He placed at the east of the Garden of Eden the cherubim”), Cain (“east of Eden”), and Moses’ cities of refuge “toward the sunrise” — so this world, which Adam entered, is east of Eden. It is puzzling, for Bava Batra 84a says the sun is red in the morning because it passes the roses of the Garden of Eden, implying Eden is in the east, and Rabbeinu Shmuel explains so there from “a garden in Eden, mikedem [eastward]”; though the Aramaic renders it “from the beginning,” it also implies east, as does Bereshit Rabba. One may answer that the verse may mean the east of Eden while Eden itself is in the west, and that the Bava Batra passage does not mean the sun literally passes there, but that in the morning, as the sun rises, a column of light falls on the chambers of the Garden of Eden in the west, and in the evening by the light of Gehenna in the east. This is not strange, since however one explains it, that passage needs such an explanation: it says there “and some say the reverse,” and it is unlikely that they disagree over whether Eden is in the east or the west. tosafot:b6.1: And mats in the days of Tishrei: The Kuntres [Rashi] explained that they placed the mats under their feet in the water because of the mud, so that it would not interpose. So it is implied in the chapter Tinoket (Niddah 66b), where Shmuel bar Rav Yitzḥak says: a woman should not immerse in a harbor; [and the Gemara explains] even though there is no mud on her now, say it fell off as she trod. After that it cites this story of Shmuel’s father, and after that what Rav Giddel said in the name of Rav: if she handed a cooked dish to her son and immersed, her immersion does not count, even though there is nothing [on her hands] now; say it fell off as she trod. Rabbeinu Tam explains “and mats” as for modesty: the rivers are small in the days of Tishrei, and he spread mats for them so that they would not be seen, lest they hurry to immerse out of embarrassment and not immerse properly. That is also the reason she should not immerse in a harbor, since people are found there and she hurries to immerse out of fear of people, similar to what it says there earlier: a woman should not stand on an earthenware vessel [to immerse], which is explained there as because she is afraid lest she fall, and does not immerse properly. [According to this,] in that teaching about the harbor we do not read “even though there is none now.”
tosafot:b6.2: In brief: “Lest the dripping exceed the flowing, and rainwater be the majority”: as the Kuntres [Rashi] explained; rainwater does not purify when flowing, as Torat Kohanim teaches: a spring purifies when flowing and a ritual bath when collected. Rabbeinu Tam says “collected” for a ritual bath is precise, excluding flowing, but “flowing” for a spring is not meant to exclude collected; rather, a spring purifies even when flowing, while a ritual bath purifies only when collected. So it is brought in Torat Kohanim: just as a spring is by the hands of Heaven, so a ritual bath must be by the hands of Heaven, excluding one made by hand from the outset; a spring purifies with any amount, a ritual bath with forty se’a; a spring purifies when flowing, a ritual bath when collected. One might bring a proof from the sea that Solomon made, in which the priests immersed although its water was gathered like a ritual bath; but that can be rejected, since the Jerusalem Talmud says it was not a vessel, the legs of the oxen being pierced like an outlet, so the water may have been flowing; and so too the ritual bath on the roof of the Parva chamber (Yoma 31a), fed by the spring of Eitam, where the High Priest immersed — the water may have entered at one side and left at the other. In any case it is plain that spring water cut off from the spring purifies when collected, for once cut off it becomes a ritual bath, as Mikvaot 5:1 teaches of a spring led over a pool and cut off; and the water of the slaughterhouse (Pesaḥim 17b), fit in the ground for immersing needles and pipes, implies collected water, like a vessel, coming from the water channel in the Temple courtyard. It seems one can bring proof even where it was not cut off from Mikvaot 8:8, cited in Shabbat 109a: Rabbi Yosei says all the seas purify when flowing but are unfit for zavim, disputing the first tanna, who says all the seas are like a ritual bath, since “the gathering of the waters He called seas.” Rabbi Yosei comes to say that although they are gathered and standing (Makkot 4a), they purify even when flowing, since the verse did not come to remove the status of flowing from them. So they dispute only flowing; all agree they purify when collected. And from what it says here, “water does not purify when flowing except the Euphrates in the days of Tishrei,” it is implied that only when flowing they do not purify, but when collected they do, even when the flowing [spring water] is not the majority. tosafot:b8.1: In brief: Water does not purify when flowing, etc.: Rabbeinu Tam explained in a responsum (beginning “Mishe-rabbu mapilei ḥalalim”) that although Shmuel, Shmuel’s father (who made ritual baths in Nisan) and Rav (“rain in the West…”) hold one view, the halakha does not follow it, but rather Shmuel’s other statement, “the river is blessed from its bed,” which the baraita “Yuval is its name” supports. Even if the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Meir and hold that Perat is its name, they still support it from his statement that its waters are fruitful and multiply, since they do not dispute that reasoning and may hold it is called Perat for that very reason; only Rabbi Meir, who has another name for it, can ask “why is it called Perat,” and for the Rabbis yuval means streams, as in “streams of water [yivlei mayim]” (Isaiah 30:25). Bereshit Rabba also expounds like Rabbi Meir: Ḥiddekel, its waters are sharp and light; Pishon, it grows flax; Perat, its waters are fruitful and multiply. Without rain, rivers and springs swell, as in Rosh HaShana 11b (in Iyyar the Pleiades rise by day and springs swell, and in Marḥeshvan they diminish because no rain fell all summer); in Pesaḥim 94b (in Tishrei, Marḥeshvan and Kislev the sun travels through the air to dry up the rivers); and in Ta’anit 25b (no handbreadth of rain descends without two handbreadths rising from below to meet it, and the upper deep says to the lower deep: let your waters well up). If you ask how we know Rav disagrees — perhaps then [in the rainy season] the river is blessed from below, as explained — the answer is: if being blessed from its bed were the ordinary way, all rivers would sometimes swell, so what witness would the Euphrates be? Rabbeinu Tam asked against Shmuel, Rav and Shmuel’s father from Para 8:10 (cited in Sanhedrin 5b): the waters of Karmiyon and Piga are unfit for the water of purification because they are mixed waters, implying that otherwise they are fit, and we do not disqualify them lest the dripping exceed the flowing. He answered that they hold these four rivers are high, for the Land of Israel is higher than all lands, and rainwater does not remain there. He asked further: according to them, in what were lepers purified, and how was water of purification sanctified on the eve of Passover (Pesaḥim 90a), or sprinkled on the men of the second Passover and on all who were impure from the dead of the wilderness, such as Mishael and Eltzafan, who were far from the Euphrates? By the answer that the four rivers are high, the immersion of zavim and lepers is not difficult, but sanctifying the water of purification and Mishael and Eltzafan still are. He answered that perhaps high rivers and channels do not get rainwater mixed into them, since rainwater runs down into the low rivers and is swept to the sea, and does not mix into high sources or into gathered water, such as rivers issuing from caves. Proof: Para 8:11 teaches that the well of Ahab and the Cave of Pamyas are fit; it had to teach this because the Jordan descends from the Cave of Pamyas and the Jordan is unfit, being mixed water, so it teaches that the Cave of Pamyas is not mixed water, while rivers and springs are fit according to all. Rabbeinu Tam also explained that by law [the rainwater] is nullified bit by bit as it comes, even for Rav and Shmuel’s father, who were stringent only for appearance’s sake on account of rain; by this last explanation none of the cases from Moses’ time are difficult, since the stringency had not yet been decreed. And it seems the rainwater is nullified in the majority, since all rivers are connected to the Great Sea, more than in the joining of ritual baths; and the rivers’ beginnings are not a sloping flow [katafres], since that is how they naturally flow; it is their living current that connects them. All this Rabbeinu Tam explained in the responsum. But the reason “bit by bit it is nullified” does not fit what was explained above (Bekhorot 22a), that any nullified prohibition reawakens when it grows back to the amount that forbids. The reason that they are connected to the Great Sea does fit; and as for Makkot 4a, where one who immerses there does not have a valid immersion, there [the waters] are present in their own right, whereas here the dripping water is not recognizable or known apart from the mixture at all. gershom:b1.1: But there are springs that are high: on the mountaintops, which appear not to come from it.
gershom:b2.1: Those are ladders of the Euphrates: that is, conduits drawn from it beneath the ground that well up on the mountaintops.
gershom:b3.1: It is the Euphrates from the beginning: that is why “it is” [hu] is written of it, to say that it comes before these.
gershom:b4.1: Its waters are fruitful and multiply: that they swell greatly.
gershom:b5.1: Is blessed from its bed: it is blessed from its banks; it grows neither from rains nor from springs, but from itself. And this disagrees with Rav, who said the Euphrates is the great witness, meaning that it grows from rains.
gershom:b6.1: And mats in the days of Tishrei: he placed them on the riverbed, since all rivers diminish in the days of Tishrei from the heat that has been, and there is mud at the bottom of the water in the riverbed; he would put the mats so that their feet would not sink into the mud and it be an interposition for the immersion. And what Shmuel said above, “the river is blessed from its bed,” disagrees with what Shmuel said, “water does not purify when flowing,” that is, water with no dripping [rain] in it but only flowing [spring water] does not purify, except the Euphrates in the days of Tishrei, since the rainwater that dripped into it has already diminished. Evidently it grows from rainwater in the days of Nisan, when the snows and the rain melt, and yet he said it grows only from its bed.
